facts.claim: Murphy and Winkler (1977), looking at US programmes where weather forecasters gave a chance of rain, found that forecasters can state such chances reliably: a stated chance comes true about that often.

Guo and colleagues (2017) found that modern neural networks, unlike those of a decade earlier, are poorly calibrated, and that temperature scaling, one number fitted on held-out data, is surprisingly effective at fixing it.

Kadavath and colleagues at Anthropic (2022) found that larger language models are well calibrated on many kinds of multiple-choice and true-or-false questions, when the questions are put to them in the right format.

OpenAI’s GPT-4 report (2023) shows its model well calibrated on part of the MMLU knowledge test before its further training with human feedback, with a calibration error of 0.007, and much less so after it, at 0.074. OpenAI’s figures, for a far larger model.
Glenn Brier proposed his score in 1950 to check weather forecasts given as probabilities: the average squared gap between each forecast and what happened.

Geifman and El-Yaniv (2017) showed how to let an already trained neural network decline some inputs: you set the error rate you can accept, and it declines the inputs it must to keep it, with high probability.

Yu and colleagues (2022) found that one temperature fitted on images pooled from many kinds left each single kind poorly calibrated: in one image test, a calibration error of about 1.1% over the pool but 5.8% within a kind.
